learning_goal: Count the ribs from the sternal angle, sort them into true, false and floating, name the three parts of the sternum, and explain why the upper ribs move like a pump handle and the lower ribs like a bucket handle.

structures.name: manubrium
structures.label: Manubrium
structures.narration: The top piece. Its upper border is the jugular notch you can feel at the root of the neck, and it takes the clavicle on each side.

structures.name: body of sternum
structures.label: Body of sternum
structures.narration: The long middle plate. It meets the manubrium at an angle that opens backwards, so the junction juts forwards as a transverse ridge you can feel through the skin — that ridge is the sternal angle.

structures.name: xiphoid process
structures.label: Xiphoid process
structures.narration: The small cartilaginous tip that ossifies late. It marks the infrasternal angle, and in chest compressions it is the landmark you stay clear of: the heel of the hand goes on the lower half of the body of the sternum, above the xiphoid, because the xiphoid can be snapped off and driven into the liver.

structures.name: right first rib
structures.label: Right rib 1
structures.narration: Short, broad and the most sharply curved. Its upper surface carries the groove for the subclavian vein in front of the scalene tubercle and the groove for the subclavian artery behind it.

structures.name: left first rib
structures.label: Left rib 1
structures.narration: Short, broad and the most sharply curved. Its upper surface carries the groove for the subclavian vein in front of the scalene tubercle and the groove for the subclavian artery behind it.

structures.name: right second rib
structures.label: Right rib 2
structures.narration: Twice as long as the first. Its cartilage meets the sternum exactly at the sternal angle, which is why counting ribs starts here.

structures.name: left second rib
structures.label: Left rib 2
structures.narration: Twice as long as the first. Its cartilage meets the sternum exactly at the sternal angle, which is why counting ribs starts here.

structures.label: Right rib 3
structures.narration: A typical true rib — head, neck, tubercle, angle, then a shaft whose lower border carries the costal groove. Its own cartilage reaches the sternum.

structures.name: right costal cartilage
structures.label: Costal cartilage (right)
structures.narration: The springy bar that carries each rib forwards. It is what lets a rib move at all — a ring of pure bone could not.

structures.label: Costal cartilage (left)

structures.name: first thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T1
structures.narration: The first rib has a single facet and articulates with this body alone. From T2 down the head spans two bodies.

structures.name: second thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T2
structures.narration: The rib fixes here behind — head to the bodies, tubercle to the transverse process. Two joints, one axis.

structures.label: Right clavicle

views.title: See it in the body
views.narration: Twelve pairs of ribs behind, the sternum in front, and the twelve thoracic vertebrae holding the whole thing at the back. It is a cage built to move — every breath changes its shape.

views.title: True, false, floating
views.narration: Ribs one to seven are true — each reaches the sternum by its own cartilage. Eight, nine and ten are false; their cartilage joins the one above. Eleven and twelve are floating and reach nothing in front.

views.title: The three parts of the sternum
views.narration: Manubrium, body, xiphoid process. Feel the jugular notch on top, run your finger down until the bone juts forwards under it as a transverse ridge — that ridge is the sternal angle.

views.title: Counting ribs from the sternal angle
views.narration: The second costal cartilage meets the sternum at the angle. Find the angle, find rib two, and count down from there — the first rib is hidden under the clavicle and cannot be counted. The angle also lies level with the disc between T4 and T5.

views.title: How a rib is fixed behind
views.narration: A typical rib holds on at two points: its head to the bodies of its own vertebra and the one above, its tubercle to the transverse process. Two fixed points make an axis, and the rib swings about that axis.

views.title: Pump handle — the upper ribs
views.narration: The upper ribs run downwards and forwards. When they rise, the sternum is pushed up and out and the chest deepens front to back — like lifting the handle of a water pump.

views.title: Bucket handle — the lower ribs
views.narration: The lower ribs swing outwards instead. Their middles lift away from the midline and the chest widens side to side — the handle of a bucket rising from the rim.

views.title: Cut across a space
views.narration: Seen from above the cage is kidney-shaped, not round, because the vertebral bodies push forward into it. The gap between two neighbouring ribs is an intercostal space — eleven on each side, each named for the rib above it.

views.title: Take the cartilage away
views.narration: Strip the cartilage and the ribs no longer reach the sternum. That elastic bar is the whole reason the cage springs: in the elderly it calcifies, the chest stiffens, and breathing costs more work.

gaps: Costal cartilage is carried as one composite model per side, so a single cartilage cannot be highlighted on its own. The catalog does hold the first to seventh cartilages individually on each side; they can replace the composite without changing a single op if per-cartilage teaching is ever needed.

The costal margin — formed by the cartilages of ribs seven to ten — therefore cannot be lit separately from the rest of the cartilage. It is taught by narration over the false-rib highlight in beat 2.

Sub-parts of a rib (head, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove) are not separate models. They are taught by narration and by the cross-section beat rather than as labelled parts. Landmark anchors were not placed because anchor coordinates must be measured on the source geometry, and a guessed anchor teaches a wrong place with full confidence.

Pump-handle and bucket-handle movement is authored as a trace along the ribs, not as animated rotation about the costovertebral axis. No op in the vocabulary moves a structure, so the motion is shown as a sequence and carried by the narration. This is the strongest candidate in the topic for the deferred diagram mode.
The thoracic inlet and the sternoclavicular joint are shown by their bones (first ribs, manubrium, clavicles) but are not separate structures; the first rib and the manubrium carry that narration.
